title: When Your Sales Team Can't Explain a Gap, You Have a Strategy Problem
documentTitle: Re: Fwd: [programmatic-news] Another header bidding push from Appnexus
emailSubject: Re: Fwd: [programmatic-news] Another header bidding push from Appnexus
excerptForBlog:
I hope all is well! In speaking with Shane yesterday, we both agree that our sales team is still having some difficulty addressing the following question from publishers: 'the only reason we are considering header bidding is because DFP / AdX does not allow other SSP demand sources to bid in real time — why don't you allow this / have you any plans on allowing it so we can better maximize yield?' The training last week was FANTASTIC and provided a ton of value to the team. However, this question was not addressed and tends to be the 'elephant in the room'. I have seen the teams lose credibility when they cannot answer this question well and I worry we are not giving consistent and accurate info to our partners.

The sales team needs to better understand our stance (and have a company approved message) on why we do not currently offer dynamic integration with other SSPs (i.e. Rubicon). I polled a few senior vertical leads, revenue account managers and SPLs and no one had a great answer to the question — 'we are only doing header-bidding to max yield across multiple demand partners, we would not do this if DFP had this capability — why don't you?' I believe we should arm the sales team with a 4-part response: (1) Empathy — explain that we understand the quickly changing market dynamics; (2) Capabilities — what we have built to protect publisher data and drive max revenue; (3) Why no dynamic calls today — tech, policy, or product prioritization issues; (4) Things to consider when choosing to adopt header bidding — latency, data leakage, complexity. I fear we are not being as effective as possible when having these conversations today and I worry about losing trust with our partners.

sourceCase: United States v. Google LLC (Ad Tech)
lessonTitle: When Your Sales Team Can't Explain a Gap, You Have a Strategy Problem
situation: In November 2015, a Google sales leader wrote internally about a recurring problem: publishers kept asking why DFP and AdX wouldn't let competing ad exchanges bid in real time — and Google's own salespeople had no good answer. The email notes that 'no one had a great answer' when polled across senior leads. Header bidding was gaining ground precisely because publishers saw Google's closed loop as the reason they needed a workaround.
insight: The hidden tension here isn't a training gap — it's a messaging gap that reveals an unresolved product stance. Google hadn't told its own team whether the absence of 'dynamic integration with other SSPs' was a technical limit, a policy choice, or a deliberate product decision. Each of those has a different honest answer. When you can't give your salespeople a clear 'why,' it usually means leadership hasn't committed to one internally. The author's proposed four-part framework — empathy, capabilities, rationale, risks of the alternative — is a smart structure, but it only works if part three ('Why no dynamic calls today') has a real, approved answer behind it. That answer is exactly what the email says the team is missing. This is a classic **competitive moat under pressure** moment: a platform's closed architecture is being challenged by an open workaround, and the company must decide whether to defend the moat, open it, or at least explain it clearly.
application: When competitors expose a gap in your product, get your internal story straight before it reaches customers. Gather your product, policy, and sales leads in one room. Force a single written answer to the hardest version of the question — not a talking-point, but a real rationale. Then give that answer to every customer-facing person before the next sales call.
pullQuote: If your frontline can't answer the obvious question, the problem isn't training — it's that you haven't decided what you actually believe.
